title: PostgreSQL: performance numbers & the write path
description: Rough throughput and scale limits to quote in an interview, why memory matters, and how a write flows through the buffer cache, WAL and indexes.
source: Study notes: when and how to use PostgreSQL in system design interviews

questions.prompt: Which step mainly gates how fast a transaction can commit?

options.text: Flushing the WAL records to disk at commit.
options.why: Right: the synchronous step before the commit is acknowledged.

options.text: Writing every dirty data page to its data file.
options.why: That happens later and asynchronously.

options.text: Rebuilding all indexes from scratch.
options.why: Indexes are updated incrementally, not rebuilt per write.

options.text: Compressing the table before the next query.
options.why: No such step exists in the commit path.

questions.explanation: Writes mutate memory first; the sequential WAL flush is the durability gate, so disk speed bounds commit latency.

questions.prompt: Why does adding more indexes lower write throughput?

options.text: Each index must be updated and generates its own WAL entries.
options.why: Right: more indexes, more work per write.

options.text: Indexes lock the whole table for the duration of a query.
options.why: Ordinary reads do not lock the table against writes.

options.text: Indexes force the data pages to be rewritten every night.
options.why: No scheduled rewriting is involved.

options.text: Indexes make rows larger so fewer fit in each row.
options.why: Index entries live in separate structures, not inside rows.

questions.explanation: Index maintenance is part of every insert and update. Keep only the indexes your queries justify.

questions.prompt: As a rough starting estimate, how many simple inserts can a single well-tuned core sustain?

options.text: Around 5,000 per second.
options.why: Right: a handy interview-level figure.

options.text: Around 5 per second.
options.why: That is far too low for a tuned node.

options.text: Around 5 million per second.
options.why: That is orders of magnitude too high for one core.

options.text: It has no relationship to the hardware used.
options.why: Hardware, especially WAL disk speed, matters a great deal.

questions.explanation: Updates with index changes run slower, around 1,000 to 2,000 per second per core. Treat all of these as rough.

questions.prompt: How do read and write throughput of a single node usually compare?

options.text: Simple indexed reads are much faster than writes.
options.why: Right: reads skip WAL and index maintenance.

options.text: Writes are roughly ten times faster than reads.
options.why: Writes carry extra durability and index work.

options.text: They are always exactly equal.
options.why: They differ because writes do more work.

options.text: Reads cannot be indexed, so they are always the slowest.
options.why: Indexes exist precisely to speed reads.

questions.explanation: Indexed lookups can reach tens of thousands per second per core, well above write rates.

questions.prompt: Roughly when do tables start to feel unwieldy and make you consider partitioning or sharding?

options.text: Past roughly 100 million rows, depending on workload.
options.why: Right: a rule of thumb, not a hard limit.

options.text: After about 10 thousand rows.
options.why: PostgreSQL handles that trivially.

options.text: Never, because size has no effect on performance.
options.why: Large tables and working sets beyond RAM clearly hurt.

options.text: Exactly at 2 billion rows, where the engine stops under normal operating conditions.
options.why: There is no such cliff.

questions.explanation: These are guides rather than limits. They tell you when to talk about partitioning, sharding and caching.

questions.prompt: True or false: keeping the frequently accessed working set in RAM is one of the biggest performance levers.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: this is why RAM and caching matter.

options.text: False
options.why: It is the reverse; memory hits are far cheaper than disk reads.

questions.explanation: Memory access is orders of magnitude faster than disk, so performance drops sharply when the working set exceeds RAM.

seriesDescription: Everything to know about PostgreSQL for system design interviews: when to pick it, SQL and ACID basics, indexing, scaling writes, replication and concurrency control, in eight short quizzes.
